```{r setup}
# Packages that need to be installed
require(dplyr)
require(tidyr)
require(naniar)
require(mice)
require(lattice)
require(flextable)
require(ggmice)
require(ggplot2)
require(patchwork)
require(forestploter)
```


```{r function forest plot}
# Function to compare later the output of the linear regression of a complete case analysis and with multiple imputation

# lm_cc and lm_mi are the output object of the lm() function 

compare_fp <- function(lm_cc, lm_mi) {
sum_mi <- summary(pool(lm_mi), conf.int = TRUE)

df_mi <- data.frame(
  variable = sum_mi$term,
  estimate_mi = sum_mi$estimate, 
  LCI_mi = sum_mi$`2.5 %`,
  UCI_mi = sum_mi$`97.5 %` )

df_cc <- as.data.frame(lm_cc$coefficients)
df_cc$variable <- rownames(df_cc)
ci <- confint(lm_cc)
df <- df_cc %>%
  rename(estimate_cc = lm_cc$coefficients) %>%
  mutate(LCI_cc = ci[, 1], 
         UCI_cc = ci[, 2]) %>%
  left_join(df_mi, by = "variable") %>%
  mutate(`Estimate (CI)`= paste0(round(estimate_cc, 2), " (", round(LCI_cc, 2), "-", round(UCI_cc, 2), ")\n", 
                                 round(estimate_mi, 2), " (", round(LCI_mi, 2), "-", round(UCI_mi, 2), ")"
  )) %>%
  slice(-1)
 df$`                       ` <- rep("", times = nrow(df))

 # setting layout specifications for the forest plot
 tm <- forest_theme(base_size = 10,
                     title_cex = 1,
                     refline_lty = "dashed",
                     #ci_pch = c(15, 18),
                     ci_col = c("#377eb8",  "orange"),
                     footnote_col = "blue",
                     legend_name = "Analysis method",
                     legend_value = c("Complete Case", "MI"),
                     legend_position = "bottom", 
                     title_just = "center") 
 
forest(df[, c(2, 8, 9)],
      est = list(df$estimate_cc, 
                 df$estimate_mi),
      lower = list(df$LCI_cc, 
                   df$LCI_mi),
      upper = list(df$UCI_cc, 
                   df$UCI_mi),
      ci_column = c(3),
      ref_line = 0, 
      theme = tm)
}
```



# Multiple Imputation with MICE

We want to analyze the prognostic impact of age, gender, BMI (centered), meat intake (proportions in previous month), education and ethnicity on systolic blood pressure using a linear regression model. We use the NHANES dataset for this (nhanesdata_v11a3.csv)

1.  Look at the missing data descriptively (only those variables which we use in our regression analysis.):

-   How many variables have missing data?
-   What is the absolute and relative frequency of missing data in each variable?
-   How is the missing data pattern?

Hint: You may use the package ggmice for visualization:

(<https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/ggmice/vignettes/ggmice.html>)


```{r}


dat <- read.csv("../data/nhanesdata_v11a3.csv")
summary(dat)

```


```{r}
# Data processing
## Format categorical variables as factors: this is important for MICE

dat <- dat %>%
mutate_at(c("educ", "ethnic", "age_cat", "meat_cat", "male2"), as.factor)%>%
select(rr_sys, age, male2, bmicenter, meat_prvmo2, educ, ethnic) %>%
filter(!is.na(rr_sys))

## get variables with missing values
## here we only get three variables that contain missing value among variables we focus on. 

colnames(dat)[colSums(is.na(dat)) != 0]

```


```{r}
## we alread selected several variable as predictors 

## get absolute and relative frequencies of missing values in each variable. 

mis_abs <- dat %>%
  summarise(across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.)),  .names = "missing_{.col}"
  )) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(),
    names_to = "Variable",
    values_to = "absolute_Count"
  )

mis_rel <- dat %>%
  summarise(across(everything(), ~
    round((sum(is.na(.))) / nrow(data) * 100, 1),
  .names = "missing_{.col}"
  )) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(),
    names_to = "Variable",
    values_to = "Relative_freq[%]"
  )

miss_freq <- merge(mis_abs, mis_rel, by = "Variable")


flextable(miss_freq) %>%
width(j = 1:3, width = 3, unit = "cm") %>%
align(j = 2:3, align = "center", part = "all")

# this is a useful package for visualization. 

```

```{r}

plot_1 <- ggmice(dat, aes(bmicenter, age)) +
   geom_point()
plot_2 <- ggmice(dat, aes(age, fill = factor(is.na(meat_prvmo2),
   labels = c("observed meat intake", "missing meat intake")
   ))) + geom_density(alpha = 0.3)

plot_1 + plot_2


plot_3 <- ggmice(dat, aes(male2)) +
geom_bar(alpha = 0.3) +
facet_wrap(~ factor(is.na(meat_prvmo2),
labels = c("observed meat intake", "missing meat intake")
))
plot_4 <- ggmice(dat, aes(male2)) +
geom_bar(alpha = 0.3) +
facet_wrap(~ factor(is.na(bmicenter),
labels = c("observed BMI", "missing BMI")
))
plot_3 + plot_4


```


```{r}
# use ggmice() to visualize the relationship between variables with/without missing values.
# See the vingette of ggmice() for the correct syntax and examples. 
# use visdat::vis_miss and md_pattern to visualize the missing data pattern


library(mice)
library(ggmice)
library(ggplot2)
library(visdat)


# 1) check complete cases
visdat::vis_miss(dat)
mice::md.pattern(dat, rotate.names = TRUE)




```

Hint: Interpretation of the output of md_pattern:

-   row: summarizes missing data patterns of observations 
(number of the left side: how many observations have missing values in this combination of variables?, number of right handside: how many variables have a missing value?)
-   which observations have missing in which variables (displayed in red)
-   numbers on the right: number of variables with missing values
-   numbers on the left: number of observations with this specific pattern of missing data




2.  We assume that the missingness mechanism is MCAR and do therefore a complete case analysis. Calculate a linear regression with age, gender, BMI (centered), meat intake (proportions in previous month), education and ethnicity as independent variables and systolic blood pressure as dependent variable. How many observations have been deleted?

```{r}

mod.cc <- lm(rr_sys~ age + male2 + bmicenter +
meat_prvmo2 + educ + ethnic,
data = dat)
summary(mod.cc)


# -> 753 observations deleted due to missingness (26%)
```

3.  Now, we want to do MICE as sensitivity analysis. 

Calculate MICE with 20 imputation using the following variables: age, gender, BMI (centered), meat intake (proportions in previous month), education and ethnicity, systolic blood pressure. 

Please note: Under normal circumstances, one would discuss for each variable with missing data the likely reason for the missingness and assess whether the missing data mechanism can be assumed to be MCAR, MAR, or MNAR. 

Based on this assessment, missing values would then be imputed using information from other observed variables that are correlated either with the missingness itself or with the variable containing missing data.)

Use the following order:

a.  Generate the prediction matrix

b.  Choose a suitable imputation method for every variable (what is the default by R?)

c.  Generate multiple imputed datasets

d.  Look at the diagnostics (did the algorithm converge? Are the imputed values plausible?

e.  Generate the prediction matrix


Hint:
-   The predictor matrix controls which variables are used to impute missing values for each incomplete variable.
    -   Rows represent the variables with missing values
    -   Columns represent the predictor variables that can be used for imputation
-   A value of 1 in the matrix means that the column variable is used as a predictor for the row variable, while 0 means it is not used



a.  Generate the prediction matrix

```{r}

# https://search.r-project.org/CRAN/refmans/mice/html/mice.html

#library(mice)

pred.matrix <- make.predictorMatrix(dat)
pred.matrix[, !(colnames(pred.matrix) %in%
c("rr_sys", "rr_dia", "educ", "bmicenter","meat_prvmo2"))] <- 0
pred.matrix

# even though bmi and educ do not need inputation, mice does it to both of them too. 
```
The predictor matrix controls which variables are used to impute missing values for each incomplete
variable.
– Rows represent the variables with missing values
– Columns represent the predictor variables that can be used for imputation
• A value of 1 in the matrix means that the column variable is used as a predictor for the row variable,while 0 means it is not used


b.  Choose a suitable imputation method for every variable (what is the default by R?)

```{r}

# See https://search.r-project.org/CRAN/refmans/mice/html/mice.html 
# which method can be applied to which data.type

meth <- make.method(dat)
# if you want to change the method:
#meth["bmicenter"] <- "norm"
# overview over available methods: ?mice (Scroll documentation down till Details) or 

methods(mice)



#pmm : Predictive Mean Matching
#polyreg: Polytomous logistic regression


```

c.  Generate multiple imputed datasets

```{r}

dat_mi1 <- mice(dat,predictorMatrix = pred.matrix,seed = 2,m = 20,maxit = 5,print = FALSE)
# take a look at completed (i.e. imputed) data set:
# complete data set 1:
head(complete(dat_mi1, action = 2), 3)

```


```{r}
# you can also convert this to a long format for data filtering, data manipulation or calculation of additional variables

long_mi <- complete(dat_mi1, action = "long", include = TRUE) # include = False, then we don't have the original data here

long_mi %>%
  dplyr::select((ncol(long_mi) - 1): ncol(long_mi), everything()) %>%
  head(5)


# back to the mids object

mids_obj <- as.mids(long_mi)

# below is the original data set, imp = 0, that is why there are NA.
# if we check imp = 1, there wont be any NA

long_mi %>% filter(.imp == 1) %>% summarise(across(everything(), ~sum(is.na(.))))

```

d.  Look at the diagnostics

```{r}

#  How did the algorithm converge? Are the imputed values plausible?

png("stripplot.png", width = 600, height = 350, res = 100)
print(stripplot(dat_mi1))
dev.off()
knitr::include_graphics("stripplot.png")


png("densityplot.png", width = 600, height = 350, res = 100)
print(densityplot(dat_mi1))
dev.off()
knitr::include_graphics("densityplot.png")


png("bwplot.png", width = 600, height = 400, res = 100)
print(bwplot(dat_mi1))
dev.off()
knitr::include_graphics("bwplot.png")

plot(dat_mi1)

# the converge by meat_provmo2 is not perfect; however, we do not take any action here.

```

4.  Re-analyse the impact of the prognostic factors on systolic blood pressure using the MI datasets.

```{r}
mod_mi1 <- with(dat_mi1,lm(rr_sys~ age + male2 + bmicenter + meat_prvmo2 + educ + ethnic))

# Display the pooled estimate, the variance decomposition in within and between variance and the FMI

pool(mod_mi1)

# pooled estimate is calculated based on Rubin's rule.
# exam: pooed estimate, variance (between and within groups)

```

5.  When we run the multiple imputation procedure with m = 5, we get for meat intake the the following coefficients and standard errors:

    | Imputation mumber | Estimate (beta) | standard error |
    |-------------------|-----------------|----------------|
    | 1                 | 0.027           | 0.0016         |
    | 2                 | 0.003           | 0.0015         |
    | 3                 | 0.032           | 0.0170         |
    | 4                 | 0.026           | 0.0160         |
    | 5                 | 0.002           | 0.0150         |
    
    Calculate the pooled beta-coefficient and the pooled standard error. You may use paper and pencil to solve this task.
    
see solution

6.  How many imputations we need for a FMI of 0.44 to have a relative efficiency of at least 0.95. Hint: The relative efficiency compares the variance of your pooled estimate with the variance you would get if you had an infinite number of imputations: $RE = \frac{Variance with infinite imputation}{Variance with finite imputation}$. This means that a relative efficiency of 0.9 means a relative increase of the variance for m imputation of $\frac{1}{0.95} = 1.052 \approx 5\%$. You may use paper and pencil to solve this task.

see solution.


7.  Compare the output of the complete case analysis and multiple imputation Hint: For the comparison, use the the function compare_fp() from line 23

```{r}

library(dplyr)
sum_mi <- summary(pool(mod_mi1), conf.int = TRUE)

df_mi <- data.frame(
  variable = sum_mi$term,
  estimate_mi = sum_mi$estimate,
  LCI_mi = sum_mi$`2.5 %`,
  UCI_mi = sum_mi$`97.5 %`
)


df_cc <- as.data.frame(mod.cc$coefficients)
colnames(df_cc)[1] <- "estimate_cc"   # 直接在这里改好列名
df_cc$variable <- rownames(df_cc)
ci <- confint(mod.cc)

df <- df_cc %>%
  mutate(LCI_cc = ci[, 1],
         UCI_cc = ci[, 2]) %>%
  left_join(df_mi, by = "variable") %>%
  mutate(`Estimate (CI)` = paste0(round(estimate_cc, 2), " (",
                                   round(LCI_cc, 2), "-", round(UCI_cc, 2),
                                   "\n",
                                   round(estimate_mi, 2), " (",
                                   round(LCI_mi, 2), "-",
                                   round(UCI_mi, 2), ")")
  ) %>%
  slice(-1)

df$` ` <- rep("", times = nrow(df))


# setting layout specifications for the forest plot
tm <- forest_theme(base_size = 10,
                   title_cex = 1,
                   refline_lty = "dashed",
                   ci_pch = c(15, 18),
                   ci_col = c("#377eb8", "orange"),
                   footnote_col = "blue",
                   legend_name = "Analysis method",
                   legend_value = c("Complete Case", "MI"),
                   legend_position = "bottom",
                   title_just = "center")

# 控制各列宽度比例
forest(df[, c(2, 8, 9)],
       est = list(df$estimate_cc,
                  df$estimate_mi),
       lower = list(df$LCI_cc,
                    df$LCI_mi),
       upper = list(df$UCI_cc,
                    df$UCI_mi),
       ci_column = c(3),
       ref_line = 0,
       theme = tm,
       # 关键参数：
       xlim = c(-3, 3),          # 手动设置 x 轴范围，根据你的数据调整
       ticks_at = c(-2, -1, 0, 1, 2),  # x 轴刻度
       widths = c(3, 1.5, 2))    # 三列宽度比例：文字列、CI文本列、图形列


```
